entities.name: Sorbonne
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Sorbonne (University of Paris) is one of the world's oldest universities, founded around 1150-1200 CE in Paris, and the mother institution from which modern Western university culture descended. For centuries the most prestigious center of theological and philosophical learning in the Christian world, the Sorbonne's faculties of theology, arts, and medicine trained the scholars, bishops, and jurists who governed medieval European civilization.

The University of Paris emerged from the cathedral schools of Notre-Dame de Paris, gaining papal recognition around 1200 CE. The Sorbonne itself — the collège de Sorbonne — was founded in 1257 by Robert de Sorbon, confessor to King Louis IX, as a residence for poor theology students. The university's conflict with the French Crown over jurisdiction and its 1229 strike (first university strike in history) established the precedent of university autonomy from secular authority.

The Sorbonne was the epicenter of medieval scholasticism: Thomas Aquinas taught there, Albertus Magnus taught there, and the Summa Theologica was developed in its intellectual environment. The university also condemned Joan of Arc in 1431 and later condemned Copernicus. The French Revolution disrupted the Sorbonne, which was closed 1793-1808. The May 1968 student uprising that triggered France's most significant modern political crisis began at Nanterre and moved to the Sorbonne, making the university permanently associated with radical student politics.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Sorbonne as medieval Europe's foremost theological university created the model for Western academic culture, hosted the development of scholasticism, and has been France's intellectual heart through revolution, Napoleon, and 1968.
